newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's bureaucrats a lightning rod for discontent.
newsitem.headline: Japan's bureaucrats a lightning rod for discontent.

text.p: Japanese politicians of all persuasions wooing voters ahead of a general election on Sunday agree on one thing -- bureaucrats make the best bogeymen.

From the conservative Liberal Democrats to the Japan Communist Party, everyone is pledging to restore political control over policy, cut bloated government agencies down to size and restructure outmoded ministries to boost efficiency.

The calls reflect the blotted copybooks of ministry mandarins after a string of policy missteps ranging from mishandling of banks' loan mess to the Health Ministry's role in a 1980s scandal over HIV-tainted blood products.

Also at work is widespread angst over whether Japan can reform the system which created the nation's postwar miracle. That system, which linked bureaucrats, big business and conservative politicians in a so-called "Iron Triangle", is now viewed by critics as a key cause of Japan's current malaise.
"Bureaucrats are performing a service for the politicians -- they're acting as a lightning rod for public discontent," said one foreign economist.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, leading his Liberal Democratic Party's (LDP) bid to win an outright victory in the election, has made bureaucratic reform a key plank in his party's platform. The LDP was booted out by a reformist coalition in August 1993 but returned to power in a coalition government formed less than a year later.

"We must carry out administrative reform," Hashimoto said in a debate kicking off the campaign. "We should cut the number of ministries by about half and make the prime minister's office an organisation that can truly exercise leadership."

Voters listening to campaign rhetoric on the issue of "administrative reform" -- a broad concept encompassing prescriptions for smaller government, fewer regulations and more political control of policy -- could be forgiven for having trouble guessing just which party was speaking.
"We must stop relying on bureaucrats and start relying on politicians," Ichiro Ozawa, head of the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), said in the same debate.

Ozawa argues that cost savings from trimming government payrolls would allow him to hold down an unpopular sales tax for now while reducing corporate and personal income taxes. Hashimoto's government has said it would raise the sales tax.
Naoto Kan, a leader of the new Democratic Party set up by defectors from the LDP's two junior partners in the ruling coalition, has perhaps the best anti-bureaucrat credentials.
Kan, a former grass-roots activist now serving as health minister, saw his popularity surge after he made good on a promise to expose the HIV-tainted blood products scandal at his ministry.
Despite the chorus of calls for reform, many analysts are sceptical about prospects for real change soon given deeply entrenched interests that favour the status quo.
Voters, meanwhile, appear more worried about their pocketbooks and pensions than bureaucratic foibles.

A poll by the business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun this week showed more voters saw economic recovery, tax reform and policy on pensions and welfare as priorities for any new government than felt administrative reform should be tackled first.

Still, even some bureaucrats admit the need for changes, including boosting bureaucratic efficiency, trimming the excessive power of the Finance Ministry -- long the pinnacle of Japan's elite agencies -- and eradicating the source of bitter inter-agency turf battles by redrawing ministry boundaries.
"The trend will be towards fewer officials and the privatisation of some functions," said one career bureaucrat.
